## Overview

`LHWR` fits local weighted regression models when observations are represented
by points on the two-dimensional Lorentz hyperboloid

\[
H^2 = \{z \in \mathbb{R}^{1,2}: \langle z,z\rangle_L = -1,\ z_0 > 0\}.
\]

The Lorentz inner product is

\[
\langle z,w\rangle_L = -z_0w_0 + z_1w_1 + z_2w_2,
\]

and the intrinsic hyperbolic distance is

\[
d_H(z,w) = \operatorname{acosh}(-\langle z,w\rangle_L).
\]

The response and predictors are ordinary real-valued variables. The geometry
enters through the local kernel weights used by the regression, so `Z` need not
be longitude-latitude coordinates. It may be a Lorentz-hyperboloid embedding
constructed from geographic, feature-map, network, functional, clinical, or
shape-based representations.

## Simulate Intrinsic Hyperbolic Heterogeneity

This example generates coefficient surfaces directly from Lorentz hyperbolic
distances. This is useful for checking whether bandwidth selection is learning
a meaningful local scale on \(H^2\).

```{r}
library(LHWR)

set.seed(20260615)

n <- 120
r_max <- 5
true_k <- 25
snr <- 8
heterogeneity <- 2

H <- simulate_H2(n, r_max = r_max, uniform_area = TRUE)
Z <- H$Z
D <- hyperbolic_distance_matrix(Z, check = FALSE)

local_h <- apply(D, 1, function(d) sort(d[d > 0])[true_k])
centers <- round(seq(10, n - 10, length.out = 5))
Phi <- sapply(centers, function(j) {
  hgwr_kernel(D[, j], local_h[j], kernel = "bisquare")
})

beta0 <- 0.4 + heterogeneity * (1.45 * Phi[, 1] - 1.25 * Phi[, 4])
beta1 <- 1.0 + heterogeneity * (1.65 * Phi[, 2] - 1.20 * Phi[, 5])
beta2 <- -0.8 + heterogeneity * (1.55 * Phi[, 3] - 1.10 * Phi[, 4])
beta_true <- cbind(Intercept = beta0, x1 = beta1, x2 = beta2)

x1 <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n)))
x2 <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n)))
eta <- beta0 + beta1 * x1 + beta2 * x2
sigma <- sqrt(var(eta) / snr)
y <- eta + rnorm(n, sd = sigma)

dat <- data.frame(y = y, x1 = x1, x2 = x2)
```

## Select a Bandwidth

For adaptive bandwidths, candidate values are neighbor counts. In this
simulation the coefficient surfaces were generated with `true_k = 25`.

```{r}
bw_cv <- bw.lhwr(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  data = dat,
  Z = Z,
  approach = "CV",
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  bandwidth_type = "knn",
  geometry = "lorentz",
  bw_grid = seq(10, 80, by = 5)
)

bw_cv
head(bw_cv$selection.table)
plot(bw_cv)
```

The selected bandwidth is chosen by the requested prediction criterion. It is
not forced to minimize coefficient error, because the true coefficients are not
known in real applications.

## Fit LHWR

```{r}
fit <- lhwr(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  data = dat,
  Z = Z,
  bw = bw_cv$bw,
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  bandwidth_type = "knn",
  geometry = "lorentz"
)

fit
summary(fit)
```

Because this is a simulation, the true coefficient surface is known and we can
compute coefficient recovery error.

```{r}
rmse_beta <- sqrt(mean(rowSums((fit$beta_hat - beta_true)^2)))
rmse_y <- sqrt(mean(fit$residuals^2))

c(RMSE_beta = rmse_beta, RMSE_y = rmse_y)
```

## Coefficient Map

```{r}
plot(fit, coefficient = "x1", Z = Z)
```

## Tangent-Space Approximation

The package also supports a tangent-space approximation. Locations are mapped
to one tangent plane with the Lorentz logarithmic map, and local weights are
computed from the positive-definite Lorentz metric induced on that tangent
plane. Equivalently, after choosing a Lorentz-orthonormal tangent basis, the
same distances can be represented as Euclidean distances in two tangent
coordinates.

```{r}
fit_tangent <- lhwr(
  y ~ x1 + x2,
  data = dat,
  Z = Z,
  bw = bw_cv$bw,
  kernel = "bisquare",
  adaptive = TRUE,
  bandwidth_type = "knn",
  geometry = "tangent"
)

fit_tangent$geometry
```

The Lorentz fit uses intrinsic hyperbolic distances for the weighting geometry.
The tangent fit is useful as an approximation and diagnostic comparison.

## Local Multicollinearity Diagnostics

LHWR uses Lorentzian kernel weights to construct local design matrices.
Therefore, local collinearity is assessed from weighted matrices

\[
X^\top W_i^{(H)} X,
\]

where \(W_i^{(H)}\) is induced by Lorentz hyperboloid distances. This follows
the classical GWR local collinearity diagnostic logic, including condition
numbers, variance inflation factors, and local weighted correlations. The
Lorentz geometry changes the local neighborhood weights, not the underlying
weighted linear algebra.

```{r}
lc <- local_collinearity(fit)
lc

head(lc$condition_number)
head(lc$local_vif)
```

Large local condition numbers or VIF values indicate that some local
coefficient estimates may be unstable because the weighted local design is
nearly collinear.
